article_title: Beyond “Treatment Versus Control”: How Bayesian Analysis Makes Factorial Experiments Feasible in Education Research
citation: Daniel Kassler, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Mariel Finucane. (2019). Beyond “Treatment Versus Control”: How Bayesian Analysis Makes Factorial Experiments Feasible in Education Research. Evaluation Review (online ahead of print). https://www.mathematica.org/publications/beyond-treatment-versus-control-how-bayesian-analysis-makes-factorial-experiments-feasible-in-education-research
title: Use Bayesian methods to make factorial experiments with many treatment arms feasible when studying complex interventions
description: The article recommends Bayesian methods as a tool for researchers studying complex interventions, because they make factorial experiments with many treatment arms vastly more feasible. As the authors conclude, "Bayesian methods are a valuable tool for researchers interested in studying complex interventions. They make factorial experiments with many treatment arms vastly more feasible." The recommendation rests on the simulation evidence of lower MDEs under hierarchical priors and partial pooling.
requirements: A research question involving multiple related interventions or implementation factors suited to a factorial design
target_learning_goals: designing adequately powered experiments to test multiple factors and factor levels
examples: The authors performed power calculations for a U.S. Department of Education experiment, simulating factorial experiments across sample sizes and treatment-arm counts.
key_sources: Daniel Kassler, Ira Nichols-Barrer, Mariel Finucane. (2019). Beyond “Treatment Versus Control”: How Bayesian Analysis Makes Factorial Experiments Feasible in Education Research. Evaluation Review (online ahead of print). https://www.mathematica.org/publications/ja-beyond-treatment-versus-control-how-bayesian-analysis-makes-factorial-experiments-feasible

article_title: Using Promotion Power to Identify the Effectiveness of Public High Schools in the District of Columbia
citation: Max Gross, Menbere Shiferaw, Jonah Deutsch, Brian Gill. (2021). Using Promotion Power to Identify the Effectiveness of Public High Schools in the District of Columbia. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs
title: Use promotion power alongside status and value-added measures when evaluating high schools
description: The study positions promotion power as a complement to existing school-effectiveness indicators: promotion power scores "are distinct from status measures such as graduation rate and college enrollment rate" because they account for prior achievement and background, and they "complement value-added measures by using similar methods to examine additional, longer-term outcomes." Districts and researchers evaluating high schools should therefore report promotion power together with, not instead of, status and value-added measures.
requirements: Prior student achievement and background data, and longer-term outcome data such as graduation and college enrollment, to estimate promotion power
constraints: Developed and illustrated for public high schools in the District of Columbia
examples: The study estimated promotion power for DC public high schools on college-ready SAT scores, high school graduation, and college enrollment as longer-term outcomes beyond value-added measures
key_sources: Max Gross, Menbere Shiferaw, Jonah Deutsch, Brian Gill. (2021). Using Promotion Power to Identify the Effectiveness of Public High Schools in the District of Columbia. Regional Educational Laboratory Mid-Atlantic, Institute of Education Sciences. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs

article_title: Technical Methods Report: Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs
citation: Peter Z. Schochet, Hanley Chiang. (2009). Technical Methods Report: Estimation and Identification of the Complier Average Causal Effect Parameter in Education RCTs. Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Use correct variance formulas when estimating the CACE parameter in education RCTs
description: The report's methodological contribution is to work out the correct variance formulas for the CACE estimator under clustered designs and to compare them with "those that are typically used in practice". Analysts estimating CACE in education RCTs should apply the correct variance formulas when assessing significance of the estimator, measured in nominal and standard deviation units.
requirements: Access to compliance information and outcome data from a clustered education RCT
constraints: The report's empirical comparison finds the variance correction terms matter little, so the practical gain from the correction may be small
target_learning_goals: correct significance testing of complier average causal effect estimates
examples: The authors compared significance findings for the CACE estimator using the correct variance formulas with those typically used in practice across ten large-scale RCTs

article_title: Improving Chicago's Schools
citation: Improving Chicago's Schools: Sample High School Summary 2005. (2005). UChicago Consortium on School Data Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Use school-specific survey reports to help a school assess its progress and plan for the future
description: The article presents the school-specific survey reports as a tool for school self-assessment and improvement planning. The reports describe a school's learning climate, instructional program, student-teacher relationships, leadership, professional environment, and community relationships. The article states that "this information about where a school is and how it is developing can help the school assess its progress and plan for the future."
requirements: Schools must meet the participation thresholds (at least 42 percent of teachers or 50 percent of students) to receive reports
target_learners: K-12 school communities in Chicago public schools
examples: Summary reports show responses on survey measures over several years; details reports show answers to specific survey questions compared across schools
key_sources: Improving Chicago's Schools: Sample High School Summary 2005. (2005). UChicago Consortium on School Data Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/improving-chicagos-schools-sample-high-school-summary-2005

article_title: Annual CPS Trend Review, 2000
citation: John Q. Easton, Todd Rosenkranz, Anthony S. Bryk. (2001). Annual CPS Test Trend Review, 2000: Elementary School Test Score Trends in Chicago Public Schools. Consortium on Chicago School Research. http://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Use mean grade equivalent scores rather than percent-at-or-above-norms indicators when reporting systemwide test trends
description: The brief argues the mean is the most sensible single statistic for reporting test score trends because it is sensitive to the performance of all included students. It states that other indicators, such as percent at or above national norms, median percentile, or median grade equivalent, "can be strongly influenced by the performance of relatively small subgroups of students."
requirements: A common inclusion standard applied consistently over the entire trend period, as the brief sets for bilingual education students.
constraints: The brief notes grade equivalents can be very sensitive to test level differences, so it re-analyzed trends using equated Rasch scores as a check.
target_learning_goals: Accurate system-level monitoring of academic achievement trends
examples: The brief reports mean ITBS grade equivalent scores by age group and race/ethnicity in Tables C and D for 1992 through 2000.

article_title: Adjusting Citywide ITBS Scores for Student Retention in Grades Three, Six, and Eight
citation: John Q. Easton, Brian Jacob, Stuart Luppescu, Melissa Roderick. (1998). Adjusting Citywide ITBS Scores for Student Retention in Grades Three, Six, and Eight. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://www.consortium-chicago.org
title: Use the mean grade equivalent, not the median or percent at norms, when examining achievement score trends over time
description: The article argues that the mean (arithmetic average) is superior for examining trends because it takes into account the performance of all students, whereas the median is most influenced by students right at the middle of the distribution and percent at or above grade level by students closest to the national average. The brief reports mean grade equivalents in Figures 1-12 while also calculating percent at or above grade level in Figure 15 for comparability with CPS reports.
requirements: Access to full score distributions so means can be computed, rather than only medians or cutoff percentages
constraints: The article acknowledges the other statistics can provide useful information about the school system; the choice is specific to examining trends and changes over time
target_learners: all tested students in a public school district
target_learning_goals: accurate interpretation of systemwide achievement trends
examples: The brief reports mean grade equivalents by grade for 1990-1998 with 1998 adjusted values (Figure 13), and shows in Figure 15 that the percent-at-norms results are similar to the mean-based results
key_sources: John Q. Easton, Brian Jacob, Stuart Luppescu, Melissa Roderick. (1998). Adjusting Citywide ITBS Scores for Student Retention in Grades Three, Six, and Eight. Consortium on Chicago School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/adjusting-citywide-itbs-scores-student-retention-grades-three-six-and-eight

article_title: MAP Growth linking studies: Intended uses, methodology, and recent studies
citation: Ann Hu, NWEA Psychometric Solutions. (2021). MAP Growth Linking Studies: Intended Uses, Methodology, and Recent Studies. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/resource/type/linking-studies/
title: Use fall and winter RIT scores to identify at-risk students early and provide tailored interventions
description: Because linking studies connect RIT scores to state proficiency levels, educators can use students' fall, winter, and early spring RIT scores to predict spring summative performance before the state test is administered. The article states that "educators can identify students who are at risk of not meeting state proficiency standards early in the year and provide tailored educational interventions or place students in the appropriate learning groups based on their entry levels." This supports programs such as Read by Grade 3.
requirements: A current linking study for the state's summative assessment
Fall, winter, or early spring MAP Growth administration
constraints: Partners are encouraged to use the projected performance level in score reports, which reflect district-specific instructional weeks
target_learners: Students in Grades 2–8, including Grade 2 students identified for Read by Grade 3 support
target_learning_goals: Meeting state proficiency standards in ELA and mathematics
examples: Grade 2 ELA linking results help educators identify students behind in reading for Read by Grade 3 programs; special studies derive RIT cuts for grade-retention decisions.
key_sources: Ann Hu, NWEA Psychometric Solutions. (2021). MAP Growth Linking Studies: Intended Uses, Methodology, and Recent Studies. NWEA. https://www.nwea.org/resource/type/linking-studies/

article_title: Avoiding bias from sum scores in growth estimates: An examination of IRT-based approaches to scoring longitudinal survey responses
citation: Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2020). Avoiding bias from sum scores in growth estimates: An examination of IRT-based approaches to scoring longitudinal survey responses. Psychological Methods. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000367
title: When estimating growth from repeated self-report survey measures, score the items with multidimensional IRT approaches that account for latent variable covariances over time rather than sum scores
description: This principle holds that longitudinal survey growth estimates are less biased when scores come from multidimensional IRT models that account for latent variable covariances over time. The article's simulations and empirical studies show such scores yield "better recovery of growth parameters relative to models using sum scores and other IRT approaches." It applies to researchers scaling psychological and social-emotional constructs across school years.
requirements: A consistent set of self-report survey items administered across multiple school years in a single-cohort repeated measure design
constraints: Advantage demonstrated relative to sum scores and other IRT approaches in the article's simulation and empirical studies; scope is psychological and social-emotional survey constructs
target_learners: elementary and middle school students surveyed on psychological and social-emotional learning constructs
target_learning_goals: accurate estimation of student growth on psychological and social-emotional constructs
examples: The authors produced scores in a single-cohort repeated measure design using sum scores and multiple IRT approaches, then compared growth parameter recovery in longitudinal growth models fitted to each set of scores.
key_sources: Megan Kuhfeld, James Soland. (2020). Avoiding bias from sum scores in growth estimates: An examination of IRT-based approaches to scoring longitudinal survey responses. Psychological Methods. https://doi.org/10.1037/met0000367

article_title: Incorporating person covariates and response times as collateral information to improve person and item parameter estimations
citation: Wang, S., & Jiao, H. (2011). Incorporating Person Covariates and Response Times as Collateral Information to Improve Person and Item Parameter Estimations. Paper presented at the annual meeting of the National Council on Measurement in Education, New Orleans, LA.
title: Use routinely collected response times and student background data as collateral information rather than discarding them as test byproducts
description: The article argues that in computer-based testing, response times, background information and academic history are "all simultaneously collected (or available) during the test administration along student responses," yet common practice ignores them. Because using RT "does not change the construct measured by a test, but increases the accuracy of estimations," testing programs should incorporate such collateral information into IRT parameter estimation for scoring, equating and scaling. The authors frame this as making tests fair by accounting for differences in personality or cognitive style among test takers, analogous to DIF analysis for gender and ethnicity.
requirements: Computerized test administration that records item-level response times and collects examinee auxiliary information
constraints: Few studies have examined the consequence of not using CI in real applications; the GLIMMIX estimation approach may fail to converge with large item counts or much missing data
target_learners: K-12 examinees in large-scale computerized assessment programs
target_learning_goals: Improved precision of person and item parameter estimates supporting scoring, equating, scaling and test quality monitoring
examples: The study compared nested joint models with and without raw score, gender and ethnicity covariates on two MPG Skills Checklist tests, finding CI models generally fit better.
key_sources: Wang, S., & Jiao, H. (2011). Incorporating Person Covariates and Response Times as Collateral Information to Improve Person and Item Parameter Estimations. article_title: Identifying students who are off-track academically in ninth grade – the role of social-emotional learning trajectories
citation: James Soland, Megan Kuhfeld. (2019). Identifying students who are off-track academically in ninth grade – the role of social-emotional learning trajectories. NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org
title: Incorporate social-emotional development trajectories into identification of students not on track for high school success
description: The article's stated implication is that early-warning identification of academically off-track students should draw on how students develop socially-emotionally, not only on academic indicators. As the summary puts it, “understanding how a student develops social-emotionally can improve identification of students not on track to succeed in high school.” The principle applies in middle school, where SEL level and growth can be measured before the 9th-grade transition.
requirements: Longitudinal SEL measures spanning middle school grades so that initial level and growth can be estimated
constraints: The page prints no evidence on how such identification should be implemented operationally
examples: The study related students' 6th-grade SEL level and 6th-to-8th-grade SEL growth to their successful transition to secondary school

article_title: The utility of adaptive testing in addressing the problem of unmotivated examinees
citation: Steven Wise. (2014). The utility of adaptive testing in addressing the problem of unmotivated examinees. Journal of Computerized Adaptive Testing, 2(1), 1–17. https://jcat.psychstat.org
title: Use computerized adaptive tests in low-stakes programs to mitigate unmotivated examinees
description: The article recommends, through its integrative review, that low-stakes testing programs address examinee motivation by using computerized adaptive tests, which it finds "can have important advantages over conventional tests" both in identifying low-effort instances and in "effectively addressing the validity threat posed by unmotivated examinees." The principle treats test format as a lever for managing examinee motivation alongside conventional test-quality work.
requirements: A computerized adaptive testing delivery platform
constraints: The advantage is stated for low-stakes testing programs where unmotivated examinees threaten score validity
target_learning_goals: Valid achievement scores despite variable examinee effort

article_title: Propensity score stratification using multilevel models to examine charter school achievement effects
citation: Beth Tarasawa, Yun Xiang. (2015). Propensity score stratification using multilevel models to examine charter school achievement effects. Journal of School Choice, 9(2), 179–196. https://www.tandfonline.com
title: Use propensity score stratification with multilevel models when estimating school achievement effects from observational data
description: When estimating the achievement effects of school transfer or school choice from non-experimental data, the article recommends combining propensity score stratification with multilevel models. The authors report that this combination "reduces selection bias which arises from confounding variables and improves the accuracy of charter school effect estimations". The multilevel component addresses the clustered structure of students within schools in cross-state samples.
requirements: Key covariates must be available to balance treatment and control groups via propensity scores
constraints: Applicable in quasi-experimental contexts; the article does not claim equivalence to randomized designs
target_learners: K-12 students in charter and traditional public schools
target_learning_goals: Accurate estimation of school effects on standardized achievement and growth
examples: The authors applied the approach to a cross-state sample of students to estimate charter school achievement and growth effects relative to traditional public schools.

Journal of School Choice, 9(2), 179–196. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/propensity-score-stratification-using-multilevel-models-to-examine-charter-school-achievement-effects/

article_title: The potential of adaptive assessment
citation: Freeman, E. (2014). The potential of adaptive assessment. Education Leadership, 71(6).
title: Use adaptive assessment results to differentiate instruction to current academic needs
description: The principle is that assessment should feed instruction directly: because computerized adaptive testing yields immediate, informative results, teachers can use them to tailor teaching. The article states that "The immediate, informative test results enable teachers to differentiate instruction to meet individual students’ current academic needs." It presents this as the instructional payoff of adopting CAT in place of uniform, factory-style testing.
requirements: An adaptive assessment that produces immediate, informative results available to teachers
constraints: The article's supporting text reports no study testing this instructional use
target_learners: K-12 students with varied current achievement levels
target_learning_goals: Instruction matched to individual students' current academic needs
examples: The article describes schools using computerized adaptive testing whose teachers receive immediate results for differentiating instruction
key_sources: Freeman, E. (2014). The potential of adaptive assessment. Education Leadership, 71(6). https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/the-potential-of-adaptive-assessment/

article_title: Evaluating the relationships between poverty and school performance
citation: Andrew Hegedus. (2018). Evaluating the Relationships Between Poverty and School Performance. NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org
title: Evaluate schools, especially high-poverty schools, using growth measures alongside achievement data because achievement alone clouds how much learning is occurring
description: The article recommends that school evaluation should not rest on achievement data alone, because "the heavy weighting of achievement data in the evaluation of U.S. schools clouds how much learning may actually be occurring." Growth measures should accompany achievement data since the study shows they offer a clearer, more accurate picture of learning, particularly for high-poverty communities. The principle applies to school-level evaluation and accountability contexts.
requirements: Both achievement data and growth measures must be available for the schools being evaluated, as the article treats achievement data as playing a critical role in tracking student progress.
constraints: The article's scope is evaluation of U.S. schools, with particular relevance to high-poverty communities.
target_learners: K-12 students in U.S. schools, particularly in high-poverty communities
target_learning_goals: Accurate evaluation of how much learning is occurring in schools
examples: The report investigates how achievement-weighted evaluation clouds learning in high-poverty communities and presents its findings through an interactive data visualization gallery.
key_sources: Andrew Hegedus. (2018). Evaluating the Relationships Between Poverty and School Performance. NWEA Research. https://www.nwea.org/research/publication/evaluating-the-relationships-between-poverty-and-school-performance/

article_title: ATS Hub Field Note — Breakthrough Innovation: A Working Definition
citation: Friedman, K., Benge-Steele, C., & Woods, A.D. (2026). ATS Field Note: Breakthrough Innovation. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/297
title: Pursue education advances through use-inspired, iterative research in partnership with practitioners and communities
description: Because education systems are structurally resistant to change, the article argues that "advances in education often depend on use-inspired, iterative research conducted in partnership with practitioners and communities." It further notes that breakthroughs can emerge not only from new ideas but from reframing entrenched problems or recombining existing capabilities in novel ways. The principle underpins the ATS Hub's vision of an infrastructure fostering a community of innovators for rapid development and scaling of breakthrough educational solutions.
requirements: Research must be use-inspired and iterative, conducted in partnership with practitioners and communities rather than detached from them
constraints: Education systems are shaped by deeply embedded norms, routines, and institutional infrastructure that resist change
target_learners: Practitioners, communities, and learners served by education innovation efforts
target_learning_goals: Developing and scaling breakthrough educational solutions addressing urgent educational challenges
examples: The ATS Hub, an IES-funded project, supports the Accelerate Transform Scale Initiative by building a field of education innovators developing use-inspired, evidence-based products harnessing emerging technologies
key_sources: Friedman, K., Benge-Steele, C., & Woods, A.D. (2026). ATS Field Note: Breakthrough Innovation. ATS Hub Field Note Series. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/297

article_title: Using Auxiliary Data to Boost Precision in the Analysis of A/B Tests on an Online Educational Platform
citation: Adam C. Sales, Ethan B. Prihar, Johann A. Gagnon-Bartsch, Neil T. Heffernan. (2023). Using Auxiliary Data to Boost Precision in the Analysis of A/B Tests on an Online Educational Platform: New Data and New Results. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 15, No 2. https://osf.io/k8ph9/
title: When analyzing A/B tests on online learning platforms, use remnant-trained imputation models for covariate adjustment alongside within-sample covariates to gain precision without sacrificing unbiasedness
description: This principle directs platform researchers analyzing randomized experiments to train outcome-prediction models on log data from non-experimental ('remnant') users and incorporate those predictions, together with within-sample covariates, into design-based covariate-adjusted estimators such as ReLOOP+. The article's summary of its findings: "covariate adjustment can lead to substantial gains in precision, with the greatest improvement resulting from adjustment using both within-sample aggregated covariates and remnant-based imputations." Because adjustment is design-based, estimates remain unbiased and inference valid even if the imputation model is poor.
requirements: Access to covariate and outcome log data from users outside the experiment (the remnant)
Randomized treatment assignment so design-based unbiasedness holds
constraints: Gains are smaller when within-sample adjustment alone already performs well; the article reports very rare cases where remnant use reduced precision
target_learners: students in online learning platforms undergoing A/B tests
target_learning_goals: precise, unbiased estimation of causal effects of educational interventions
examples: The article compared T-Test, LOOP, ReLOOP, and ReLOOP+ across 227 randomized ASSISTments contrasts and found remnant-based estimators consistently outperformed those using only within-sample covariate adjustment
key_sources: Adam C. Sales, Ethan B. Prihar, Johann A. Gagnon-Bartsch, Neil T. Heffernan. (2023). Using Auxiliary Data to Boost Precision in the Analysis of A/B Tests on an Online Educational Platform: New Data and New Results. article_title: Teaching Strategies for Improving Algebra Knowledge in Middle and High School Students
citation: Star, J. R., Caronongan, P., Foegen, A., Furgeson, J., Keating, B., Larson, M. R., Lyskawa, J., McCallum, W. G., Porath, J., & Zbiek, R. M. (2015). Teaching strategies for improving algebra knowledge in middle and high school students (NCEE 2015-4010). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Use solved problems to engage students in analyzing algebraic reasoning and strategies
description: This recommendation has teachers present worked examples showing both the problem and the solution steps, and have students discuss and analyze the structures, steps, and reasoning rather than only producing answers. The rationale is that "Solved problems can minimize the burden of abstract reasoning by allowing students to see the problem and many solution steps at once—without executing each step—helping students learn more efficiently." Implementation steps include discussing solved problem structures, selecting problems matched to the lesson's aim including common errors, and using whole-class discussion, small-group work, and independent practice with incomplete or alternating solved problems.
requirements: Solved problems should reflect the lesson's instructional aim, and incorrect solved problems must be clearly labeled so students do not confuse correct and incorrect strategies
constraints: The guide rates the supporting evidence Minimal; the studies meeting WWC standards did not examine solved problems across different situations, so broader use rests on panel belief
target_learners: Students in remedial, regular, and honors algebra classes in grades 6-12
target_learning_goals: Analyzing algebraic reasoning and solution strategies
Developing deeper understanding of solution processes
examples: Teachers present parallel correct and incorrect solved problems for factoring and completing the square, with probing questions guiding discussion of strategic and procedural errors
Independent practice alternates a solved problem with a similar unsolved problem so students use the worked example to guide their own work

article_title: Linking Social-Emotional Learning to Long-Term Success
citation: Can Student Surveys About Social-Emotional Development and School Climate Reveal Which High Schools Best Support Social-Emotional Development? (2019). Education Next. https://www.educationnext.org
title: Use social-emotional survey measures alongside traditional indicators like test scores for a more complete picture of school performance
description: The article recommends combining student survey measures of social-emotional development with traditional academic indicators when evaluating how schools prepare students. It states that "these surveys can be used alongside traditional indicators like test scores to provide a more complete picture of how schools prepare students for the future." Because social-emotional value-added is nearly as predictive of schools' test-score impacts as test-score value-added itself, the two kinds of measures capture complementary information about school quality.
requirements: A detailed annual survey about social-emotional development and school climate administered to students, plus value-added analysis to identify school effects
constraints: The authors describe the analysis as an important early step toward understanding how schools influence social-emotional development and how it can be useful for policy
target_learning_goals: social-emotional development and academic preparation for future outcomes
examples: Chicago Public Schools administered a detailed annual survey about social-emotional development and school climate, and the authors used value-added analysis to identify schools' impacts on social-emotional development and test scores
key_sources: Can Student Surveys About Social-Emotional Development and School Climate Reveal Which High Schools Best Support Social-Emotional Development? (2019). Education Next. https://www.educationnext.org

article_title: High School GPAs and ACT Scores as Predictors of College Completion
citation: Allensworth, E. M., & Clark, K. (2019). High School GPAs and ACT Scores as Predictors of College Completion: Examining Assumptions about Consistency across High Schools. University of Chicago. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/high-school-gpas-and-act-scores-as-predictors-of-college-completion
title: Use HSGPAs formatively to guide school improvement and college-readiness efforts, and rely less heavily on individual test scores
description: The article recommends that schools and districts treat grades as the primary actionable indicator of college readiness because HSGPAs are strongly related to college completion at all high schools, while individual ACT scores add little signal beyond school effects. It states this research "strongly supports the use of students' grades in a formative way, to guide school improvement efforts and assess the effectiveness of programs designed to improve college readiness, and relying less heavily on test scores." States and districts are also advised to weigh test scores less in accountability systems.
requirements: Longitudinal data systems that allow tracking of students' actual college performance, so schools do not rely solely on test scores as readiness indicators
constraints: Evidence comes from Chicago public school graduates enrolling in four-year colleges; the authors note results could differ with a more comprehensive sample
target_learners: high school students preparing for college
examples: The study found programs that raise test scores do not always raise grades, and schools improving test scores are not always those improving grades, supporting grade-based formative evaluation

article_title: Using the EQUIP Observation Tool to Advance Equity in Math Classrooms
citation: Cunningham, J., Takahashi, S., & Hirschboeck, K. (2024). Using the EQUIP observation tool to advance equity in math classrooms. WestEd. https://WestEd.org
title: Use EQUIP with a partner or team rather than independently
description: The interviewed researchers and teachers found it hard to envision a teacher using EQUIP alone, citing "real constraints on teachers' time." They recommend working in grade-level or department teams to collect and make sense of data together, which strengthens relationships, sustains focus on equitable participation, and mitigates difficult emotions the data can surface, since no single individual is to blame for inequitable participation.
requirements: Support from an instructional coach, school leader, paraprofessional, or research partner to help collect data
constraints: A research team and swivel camera are not necessary; support can come from other school staff
target_learners: teachers and instructors using EQUIP in mathematics classrooms
examples: PIRT participants were paired to observe each other's classes; John said watching another instructor's classroom with feedback guidance was the most powerful part
Sophia used EQUIP with her co-teacher through the ARISE project

article_title: A Critical Narrative Synthesis of Psychological Correlates, Measurement, and Reported Findings on Conversational AI Engagement and Dependence-Related Constructs
citation: Yan D (2026). A critical narrative synthesis of psychological correlates, measurement, and reported findings on conversational AI engagement and dependence-related constructs. Front. Psychol. 17:1827795. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1827795
title: Provisional framework separating use orientation (instrumental-cognitive vs. relational-emotional) from regulation
description: An interpretive, hypothesis-generating framework organizing conversational-AI engagement along two questions: what users seek (use orientation: mainly instrumental-cognitive or relational-emotional) and how regulated their engagement remains (calibrated vs. increasingly difficult to control). The article states: "At the level of use orientation, engagement may be mainly instrumental-cognitive or relational-emotional." Either orientation may be useful, compensatory, or dysregulated. It was developed during synthesis, not preregistered, and is not a validated factor structure, causal pathway, or developmental sequence.
requirements: Requires independent testing of its temporal ordering, cultural stability, and platform specificity before use as a measurement or causal model
constraints: Not a validated factor structure, causal pathway, or clinical model; developed from the same corpus it organizes and not tested against an independent evidence set
target_learners: Researchers and designers studying conversational-AI use, including student and higher-education users
target_learning_goals: Distinguishing instrumental-cognitive from relational-emotional AI use and calibrated from dysregulated engagement
examples: The synthesis coded 22 first-order empirical records into relational-emotional engagement (13), dysregulated dependence (5), and instrumental-cognitive reliance (4) domains
key_sources: Yan D (2026). A critical narrative synthesis of psychological correlates, measurement, and reported findings on conversational AI engagement and dependence-related constructs. Front. Psychol. 17:1827795. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1827795

article_title: ‘Models of’ versus ‘Models for’
citation: Gouvea, J., Passmore, C. (2017). 'Models of' versus 'Models for'. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-017-9884-4
title: Use the models of versus models for heuristic to notice and interpret how models are positioned in standards, curriculum, and classrooms
description: The article recommends that educators apply the models of versus models for contrast as an interpretive lens. Rather than treating models only as representations of phenomena, educators should attend to the aims and intentions models serve when enacting the modeling practice in science classrooms. The authors frame this as a way to examine the role the practice of developing and using models plays in science and how it can be leveraged in a science classroom.
requirements: Educators must have access to standards, curriculum, and classroom instances of modeling to which the heuristic can be applied.
constraints: The article presents the heuristic as a lens for noticing and interpreting, not as a validated instructional procedure.
target_learning_goals: Meaningful engagement in the scientific practice of developing and using models
examples: The authors present the heuristic in response to the inclusion of developing and using models in the Framework for K-12 Science Education and the Next Generation Science Standards.
key_sources: Gouvea, J., Passmore, C. (2017). 'Models of' versus 'Models for'. Science & Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11191-017-9884-4

article_title: Interaction in Distance Education and Online Learning: Using Evidence and Theory to Improve Practice
citation: Abrami, P.C., Bernard, R.M., Bures, E.M., Borokhovski, E., Tamim, R.M. (2012). Interaction in Distance Education and Online Learning: Using Evidence and Theory to Improve Practice. In: Moller, L., Huett, J. (eds) The Next Generation of Distance Education. Springer, Boston, MA. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4614-1785-9_4
title: Use interaction evidence and theory to improve distance and online learning practice
description: The chapter argues that research evidence and theory on interaction should be used to improve distance and online learning practice: the authors "suggest how these results may foster instructional improvement". Meta-analytic findings on the three interaction types are treated as a basis for design decisions rather than merely descriptive results.
requirements: Instructional designers should attend to the three interaction types identified by the meta-analytic evidence
constraints: Methodological issues in the underlying research need to be considered when applying the findings

article_title: FREQUENCY EFFECTS IN LANGUAGE PROCESSING
citation: Nick C. Ellis. (2002). Frequency Effects in Language Processing: A Review with Implications for Theories of Implicit and Explicit Language Acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 24, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263102002024
title: Usage-based exemplar theory of language acquisition
description: The review endorses usage-based theories in which "the acquisition of language is exemplar based". Acquisition proceeds as "the piecemeal learning of many thousands of constructions and the frequency-biased abstraction of regularities within them", so that "The regularities of language emerge from experience as categories and prototypical patterns". The article uses this framework to interpret the frequency effects it documents and to explain the developmental sequence of second language acquisition.
requirements: Learners must be exposed to substantial input, since regularities are abstracted in a frequency-biased way from experienced exemplars.
target_learning_goals: acquisition of constructions, categories, and prototypical patterns of the target language
key_sources: Nick C. Ellis. (2002). Frequency Effects in Language Processing: A Review with Implications for Theories of Implicit and Explicit Language Acquisition. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 24, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263102002024

article_title: Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations
citation: Klaus Krippendorff. (2004). Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations. Human Communication Research 30, 3: 411-433. https://astro.temple.edu/~lombard/carman.htm
title: Use only chance-corrected agreement coefficients satisfying interchangeability and population-reference conditions; reject %-agreement, correlation, and association measures as reliability indices
description: The article recommends inferring reliability only from chance-corrected agreement coefficients that treat coders as interchangeable and refer to the population of data. It states: "The use of %-agreement should be actively discouraged, especially as a fallback criterion." Association, correlation, and consistency coefficients, Cohen's kappa, Benini's beta, Cronbach's alpha, and %-agreement should be rejected as incompatible with reliability concerns. Alpha, applicable to multiple coders and many metrics including missing data and small samples, is offered as the general choice, reducing to Scott's pi for two coders, large samples, and nominal data.
requirements: A decisive coefficient must measure agreements within multiple descriptions regardless of numbers and kinds of coders
constraints: Kappa should be restricted to reliability studies in which one pair of coders judges all units and unequal coder preferences are not problematic, per Fleiss
target_learning_goals: testing the reproducibility of data-making processes
examples: Figure 2 derives the dichotomous forms of seven coefficients, and the recommendations section names which to reject and which to prefer
key_sources: Klaus Krippendorff. (2004). Reliability in Content Analysis: Some Common Misconceptions and Recommendations. Human Communication Research 30, 3: 411-433. https://astro.temple.edu/~lombard/carman.htm

article_title: Synthesizing frameworks of higher education student learning outcomes
citation: Markle, R., Brenneman, M., Jackson, T., Burrus, J., & Robbins, S. (2013). Synthesizing Frameworks of Higher Education Student Learning Outcomes. ETS Research Report Series, ETS RR-13-22. http://search.ets.org/researcher
title: USDOL-ETA General Competency Model Framework
description: The U.S. Department of Labor's Employment and Training Administration developed a competency model to determine worker requirements based on employer and business needs. "The competencies included in this framework are represented by nine tiers, organized in a hierarchical, or stackable fashion, with general competencies at the bottom and job-specific competencies at the top". Lower tiers are broad foundation competencies applicable across industries; upper tiers cover occupation-specific knowledge and management competencies.
requirements: Designed to represent the skills of employees rather than the knowledge, skills, abilities, and mindset of a well-rounded citizen
constraints: Work-contextualized: tiers 4-5 are sector- or industry-specific and tiers 6-9 are occupation-specific, so the model does not span all fields as a higher education framework would
target_learners: workers and workforce entrants, including those holding 4-year degrees
examples: Foundation competencies include initiative (personal effectiveness), mathematics (academic), and teamwork (workplace) applicable across many industries
key_sources: Markle, R., Brenneman, M., Jackson, T., Burrus, J., & Robbins, S. (2013). Synthesizing Frameworks of Higher Education Student Learning Outcomes. ETS Research Report Series, ETS RR-13-22. http://search.ets.org/researcher

article_title: Measuring problem solving skills via stealth assessment in an engaging video game
citation: Shute, V. J., Wang, L., Greiff, S., Zhao, W., & Moore, G. (2016). Measuring problem solving skills via stealth assessment in an engaging video game. Computers in Human Behavior, 63, 106-117. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2016.05.047
title: Use Your Brainz stealth assessment with 32 indicators and per-level Bayesian networks
description: Use Your Brainz is a slightly modified version of Plants vs. Zombies 2 in which stealth assessment was embedded via Glasslab's access to the source code. The assessment uses 32 in-game indicators (7 for analyzing givens and constraints, 7 for planning, 14 for tool use, 4 for monitoring and evaluating progress), scored into discrete states and linked to competency variables through conditional probability tables configured using Samejima's graded response model. A unique Bayes net was built for each of 42 levels across two worlds, updating estimates in real time from log-file evidence.
requirements: Log-file telemetry capturing the indicator events, and CPT parameters initially set by experts and calibrated with pilot data
constraints: Discrimination estimates were set low (e.g., 0.3 for indicator #37) because game-based assessment involves many confounds such as prior gameplay experience
target_learning_goals: problem solving skill measurement across four facets
examples: Indicator #37 scores planting Iceberg Lettuce within a Snapdragon's attack range as an inversely coded ratio binned into very good/good/ok/poor states
key_sources: Shute, V. J., Wang, L., Greiff, S., Zhao, W., & Moore, G. (2016). Measuring problem solving skills via stealth assessment in an engaging video game. Computers in Human Behavior, 63, 106-117. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2016.05.047

article_title: Visual processing speed
citation: Owsley Cynthia. (2012). Visual Processing Speed. Vision Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.visres.2012.11.014
title: Useful field of view (UFOV) construct
description: The useful field of view is the spatial area over which useful information can be acquired rapidly within a single fixation, without eye or head movements. The review states Ball and Roenker "defined the useful field of view as the spatial area over which useful information can be acquired rapidly without the use of eye or head movements (within one fixation)". Its size is not fixed but depends on stimulus configuration and task demands, including foveal load, distractor presence and similarity, and age. It underpins both the clinical UFOV assessment and the speed-of-processing training program.
requirements: Assessment requires brief stimulus displays challenging the observer's processing abilities, with central and peripheral tasks under divided-attention and distractor conditions
constraints: The review notes the construct's size "depends on the situation (stimulus configuration and task demands)", so it is not a fixed sensory field measure
target_learning_goals: visual processing speed under divided attention and visual clutter
examples: The original test used three subtests with high-contrast targets, display durations of 16.67 to 250 ms, and peripheral targets at 10°, 20°, or 30° eccentricity along 8 radial directions
key_sources: Owsley Cynthia. (2012). Visual Processing Speed. Vision Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.visres.2012.11.014

article_title: Self-regulated strategy development’s effectiveness: underlying cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms
citation: Jonathan Fernandez, Jessica Guilbert. (2024). Self-regulated strategy development's effectiveness: underlying cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms. Metacognition and Learning (2024) 19:1091–1135. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09398-7
title: Use knowledge of SRSD's underlying mechanisms and moderating factors to target teaching emphasis, monitor skills, and design adaptive scaffolding
description: The article argues that understanding why, how, and for whom SRSD works should directly shape classroom practice. Insight into the intervention's cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms and the factors that might hinder it "could help enhance teachers' use of SRSD by providing clear recommendations on (1) the aspect of the intervention they should emphasize to their students, (2) which skills to monitor to identify students' difficulties and adjust their teaching if needed". This supports differentiated support, such as adaptive scaffolding for students whose working memory limits strategy implementation.
requirements: Teachers need knowledge of which cognitive and motivational factors moderate SRSD's effectiveness to identify students' difficulties
constraints: The article notes some students, particularly those with poor working memory, struggled to implement the taught planning strategies, indicating a need for adjusted teaching
target_learners: elementary school students receiving SRSD writing instruction
examples: The study assessed working memory, graphomotor skills, self-efficacy, and writing motivation before the lessons to determine whether these factors moderated the intervention's effectiveness.
key_sources: Jonathan Fernandez, Jessica Guilbert. (2024). Self-regulated strategy development's effectiveness: underlying cognitive and metacognitive mechanisms. Metacognition and Learning (2024) 19:1091–1135. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09398-7

article_title: Learning Stories Through Gesture: Gesture’s Effects on Child and Adult Narrative Comprehension
citation: Dargue, N; Sweller, N. (2020). Learning Stories Through Gesture: Gesture's Effects on Child and Adult Narrative Comprehension. Educational Psychology Review, 32 (1). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09505-0
title: Educators should use typical, frequently produced iconic gestures that are adequately semantically related to speech to enhance student understanding
description: This principle translates the article's findings into educator practice: when narrating stories or explaining content, speakers should produce typical, frequently produced iconic gestures that are adequately semantically related to their speech. The article argues that "educators' use of typical, frequently produced iconic gestures that are adequately semantically related to speech may enhance student understanding." The recommendation follows from the finding that typical, not atypical, gestures benefited narrative comprehension across child and adult learners.
requirements: Gestures must be typical and frequently produced
Gestures must be adequately semantically related to the accompanying speech
constraints: The article hedges the benefit with "may enhance student understanding"
target_learners: Children and adults in educational settings
target_learning_goals: Narrative comprehension and understanding of spoken content
examples: Across two studies, observing typical gestures during narrated stories significantly benefited narrative comprehension compared with atypical or no gestures.
key_sources: Dargue, N; Sweller, N. (2020). Learning Stories Through Gesture: Gesture's Effects on Child and Adult Narrative Comprehension. Educational Psychology Review, 32 (1). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09505-0

article_title: The Relationship between Visuospatial Working Memory and Mathematical Performance in School-Aged Children: a Systematic Review
citation: Katie Allen & Steve Higgins & John Adams. (2019). The Relationship between Visuospatial Working Memory and Mathematical Performance in School-Aged Children: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09470-8
title: Researchers should use standardised mathematics measures when investigating the VSWM–mathematics relationship
description: This principle directs researchers studying the VSWM–mathematics relationship to prefer standardised mathematics assessments over study-specific measures, because the review found the choice of measure significantly influences the estimated effect size. The review states that "researchers ought to be cautious of devising their own measures of mathematics attainment where a suitable standardised measure is available." It applies to study design in research on cognitive predictors of mathematics attainment.
requirements: A suitable standardised mathematics measure must be available for the age group and mathematics domain being studied
constraints: The finding concerns effect-size estimation in correlational studies of VSWM and mathematics, not instructional outcomes
target_learners: school-aged children aged 0–16 in mainstream schools
target_learning_goals: mathematics performance (numerical operations and mathematical reasoning)
examples: The review's subsection analysis compared mean effect sizes of 0.44 for standardised versus 0.25 for unstandardised mathematics measures across 35 studies
key_sources: Katie Allen & Steve Higgins & John Adams. (2019). The Relationship between Visuospatial Working Memory and Mathematical Performance in School-Aged Children: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09470-8

article_title: Evidence based approaches for enhancing vocational education worldwide
citation: Dragos Iliescu, Samuel Greiff & Andrei Ion. (2025). Evidence based approaches for enhancing vocational education worldwide. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00317-2
title: Use PISA-VET results for targeted reform and collaboration, not merely league-table benchmarking
description: The article recommends that stakeholders interpret PISA-VET data "in a way that drives meaningful change in vocational education" rather than treating it as a benchmarking exercise. Proposed uses include deep analysis of strengths and weaknesses in specific competencies for targeted curricular reform, sharing best practices internationally, standardizing or aligning VET curricula, and engaging industry partners to translate findings into actionable insights.
requirements: Stakeholder focus on meaningful interpretation of data
Engagement with industry partners in interpreting findings
constraints: League-table misuse is identified as a common problem with international large-scale assessments such as PISA
target_learning_goals: Alignment of education with labor-market demands
examples: The article proposes deep analysis of results to highlight strengths and weaknesses in specific competencies, enabling targeted reforms in curricula and teaching methods
key_sources: Dragos Iliescu, Samuel Greiff & Andrei Ion. (2025). Evidence based approaches for enhancing vocational education worldwide. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00317-2

article_title: A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education
citation: Kaśka Porayska‑Pomsta. (2024). A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 73–83. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00346-1
title: Build AIED systems with user control over system operation as critical to their adaptive potential
description: The article argues that exposure to differently abled learners and non-mainstream contexts spotlights "the necessity to extend our field of view" and "to consider certain dimensions, such as user control over the operation of the systems we build, as critical to the adaptive potential of those systems." The principle directs designers to build learner agency, control and ownership — as instantiated in Open Learner Models — into AIED systems, because typicality-based overlay models can produce inflexible designs where users must adapt to the technology rather than the reverse. The article cites Bull & Kay (2016) for an AIED-centric perspective on user control.
requirements: Designs must give users degrees of agency, control and ownership over system-generated data and learning processes, as in Open Learner Models
constraints: The extent to which qualitative and interpretivist methods alone can inform generalisable conclusions and standardised approaches remains, by the article's own statement, an open question
target_learners: learners in special educational needs contexts
examples: The article points to AIED supports that facilitate pro-active help-seeking by students and students' self-reporting on their emotional states in collaborative or exploratory settings as ways tailoring can give learners greater agency
key_sources: Kaśka Porayska‑Pomsta. (2024). A Manifesto for a Pro-Actively Responsible AI in Education. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 34, 73–83. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00346-1

article_title: Improving workplace-based assessment and feedback by an E-portfolio enhanced with learning analytics
citation: van der Schaaf, M., Donkers, J., Slof, B., Moonen-van Loon, J., van Tartwijk, J., Driessen, E., Badii, A., Serban, O., Ten Cate, O. (2016). Improving workplace-based assessment and feedback by an E-portfolio enhanced with learning analytics. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-016-9496-8
title: Design learning-analytics feedback through the eyes of the users, with privacy safeguards
description: The article concludes that analytics-enhanced assessment design succeeds only when developed and implemented through the eyes of the users: "Only a close cooperation between the community of practitioners and technical partners will ensure a sound implementation of an easy accessible E-portfolio environment" with personalized feedback modules. Because E-portfolio data is multi-sourced, ethical safeguards are required: learners as data owners must grant access via informed consent procedures, and "the E-portfolio data has to be anonymized before analysing it in the student model". When the human factor is neglected, personalized feedback may be incorrect or misinterpreted, with undesirable and unethical impact.
requirements: Informed consent forms and a sound procedure must be formalized for learner, supervisor and researcher access to E-portfolio data
Personalized feedback must be aligned with the ethics of the field and with the needs and characteristics of the users
constraints: The article warns that improper attention to the human factor can lead to incorrect or easily misinterpreted feedback with unethical impact on the user
target_learners: students, supervisors and researchers in workplace-based professional education
target_learning_goals: trustworthy, ethically sound personalized feedback and assessment at the workplace
examples: In the project, portfolio data updates sent to the student model API were anonymized and a procedure for privacy-enhanced user identities was applied
key_sources: van der Schaaf, M., Donkers, J., Slof, B., Moonen-van Loon, J., van Tartwijk, J., Driessen, E., Badii, A., Serban, O., Ten Cate, O. (2016).
