article_title: Utilising mobile game based learning methods effectively to support education
citation: Nisiotis, L. (2021). Utilising mobile game based learning methods effectively to support education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09887-x
title: When adopting mobile game-based learning, draw on systematic review findings to guide effective utilisation of mGBL approaches
description: The article recommends that decisions about using mobile game-based learning be grounded in the accumulated findings of review scholarship rather than ad hoc choices. It presents its response as "highlighting how practitioners, scholars and designers can use their findings to effectively utilise mobile Game Based Learning (mBGL) approaches to support and enhance learning", treating the 13-year review as a practical resource for designing and deploying mGBL.
requirements: Access to the review findings of Giannakas et al. (2018) on 13 years of mobile game-based learning
constraints: The article addresses utilisation of mGBL approaches specifically; it does not claim the review findings transfer to non-mobile or non-game contexts
target_learners: practitioners, scholars and designers of mobile game-based learning
target_learning_goals: effective utilisation of mobile game-based learning to support and enhance learning
examples: The article structures its response around the key ideas of the Giannakas et al. (2018) review, read from a practical perspective for mGBL use
key_sources: Nisiotis, L. (2021). Utilising mobile game based learning methods effectively to support education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09887-x

article_title: Efficacy of a map on search, orientation and access behaviour in a hypermedia system
citation: Stanton, N., Correia, A. P. and Dias, P. (1997). Efficacy of a map on search, orientation and access behaviour in a hypermedia system. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Efficacy+of+a+map+on+search+orientation+and+access+behaviour+in+a+hypermedia+system
title: Design hypermedia for fundamental usability rather than adding map-based navigational aids
description: The article recommends that designers of non-linear learning environments address usability rather than navigation: designers "should be addressing the usability of their systems" instead of seeking more complex navigational information. It argues navigational aids are "a symptom of poor design" and that simplicity of interface plus tools supporting users' actions, such as bookmarks and simple forward, back and home buttons, may serve learners better than map-based navigation built on the spatial metaphor.
requirements: Hypermedia environments should provide users with appropriate cues at the decision points within the interaction
constraints: Navigational aids are characterized as symptoms of the current ills of hypertext rather than cures
target_learning_goals: efficient and purposeful access to task-relevant information in non-linear learning environments
examples: The study concluded that greater map use led to less relevant searching behaviour and less effective search effort, prompting the recommendation to focus on fundamental usability
key_sources: Stanton, N., Correia, A. P. and Dias, P. (1997). Efficacy of a map on search, orientation and access behaviour in a hypermedia system. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Efficacy+of+a+map+on+search+orientation+and+access+behaviour+in+a+hypermedia+system

article_title: Does Hands-On Science Practices Make an Impact on Achievement in Science? A Meta-Analysis
citation: Caglak, S. (2017). Does hands-on science practices make an ımpact on achievement in science? A meta-analysis. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 3(1), 69-87. https://www.jeseh.net
title: Use hands-on activities as an effective strategy for teaching science
description: The article's implication is that hands-on science activities, in which students actively manipulate materials while learning science, should be employed in science teaching to support achievement and scientific literacy. The author states "Our findings also suggest that hands-on activities be used for effective science teaching" and that educators are responsible to employ or encourage their use during science teaching. The recommendation rests on the meta-analytic overall effect estimate, which the author himself flags as possibly inflated by publication bias.
requirements: Activities must involve students actively manipulating objects and variables, performing experiments, making observations, collecting and recording data, reasoning, and sharing findings, as the included interventions did
constraints: The evidence base is limited to Turkish studies between 2000 and 2015 meeting the inclusion criteria; the author states "This analysis was limited with studies conducted only in Turkey"
Some previous studies found no advantage of hands-on over virtual materials or paper-and-pencil tasks, and the author notes cognitive manipulation of variables may be the crucial ingredient
target_learners: Middle school, high school and college/university students in science courses
target_learning_goals: Science achievement (conceptual understanding and performance in science sub-disciplines)
Scientific literacy and scientific inquiry skills
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 15 Turkish experimental studies in which hands-on activities were the intervention compared against teacher-centered or lecture-based instruction, with achievement tests as the outcome measure
key_sources: Caglak, S. (2017). Does hands-on science practices make an ımpact on achievement in science? A meta-analysis. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 3(1), 69-87. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1125775

article_title: Meta-Analysis on the Effectiveness of Using the Drama Approach in Social Studies Course
citation: Yildirim, E., Tikman, F., & Senturk, M. (2022). Meta-analysis on the effectiveness of using the drama approach in social studies course. International Journal on Social and Education Sciences (IJonSES), 4(1), 17-33. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijonses.301
title: Use the drama approach as an effective method for teaching social studies
description: Based on the meta-analytic finding of a strong positive effect of drama on social studies achievement, the authors conclude that drama is an effective teaching method in this domain. They state that "teachers and researchers should make use of this method for teaching in social studies lessons". The recommendation rests on the pooled effect of drama versus traditional teaching across 31 studies.
requirements: Experimental or quasi-experimental use of drama within the social studies course, as in the included studies
constraints: Evidence base is limited to primary and secondary school students in the Turkish sample (1999–2021); only 2 of the 31 studies were PhD theses
target_learners: Primary and secondary school students in social studies courses
examples: The meta-analysis pooled 38 effect sizes from 31 studies in which experimental groups were taught with the drama approach and control groups with traditional methods
key_sources: Yildirim, E., Tikman, F., & Senturk, M. (2022). Meta-analysis on the effectiveness of using the drama approach in social studies course. International Journal on Social and Education Sciences (IJonSES), 4(1), 17-33. https://doi.org/10.46328/ijonses.301

article_title: Realistic Mathematics Education and Mathematical Literacy: A Meta-Analysis Conducted on Studies in Indonesia
citation: Amelia Defrianti Putri, Dadang Juandi, Turmudi. (2024). Realistic mathematics education and mathematical literacy: a meta-analysis conducted on studies in Indonesia. Journal of Education and Learning (EduLearn), Vol. 18, No. 4. https://doi.org/10.11591/edulearn.v18i4.21650
title: Use realistic mathematics education to improve students' mathematical literacy proficiency
description: The article recommends that mathematics educators adopt RME as a means of improving students' proficiency in mathematical literacy. RME involves students beginning learning by "engaging with authentic scenarios and real-world challenges" and reconstructing mathematical concepts with the teacher's assistance. The recommendation rests on the meta-analysis's pooled large positive effect (g = 1.031) across seventeen Indonesian experimental studies.
requirements: RME is implemented as an intervention contrasted with conventional learning, as in the included experimental studies
constraints: Evidence base is limited to Indonesian studies published 2014–2023 using experimental designs with control groups
target_learners: primary, middle, and high school students in Indonesia
examples: The meta-analysis pooled seventeen studies in which RME classes were compared with conventionally taught control classes on mathematical literacy measures.
key_sources: Amelia Defrianti Putri, Dadang Juandi, Turmudi. (2024). Realistic mathematics education and mathematical literacy: a meta-analysis conducted on studies in Indonesia. Journal of Education and Learning (EduLearn), Vol. 18, No. 4. https://doi.org/10.11591/edulearn.v18i4.21650

article_title: Impact of extended reality on robot-assisted surgery training: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Bickford Michael, Alruwaili Fayez, Ragab Sara, Rothenberg Hanna, Abedin-Nasab Mohammad (2025). Impact of extended reality on robot-assisted surgery training: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02559-z
title: Use extended reality simulators as a low-cost, low-risk environment for training robotic surgery novices
description: The article supports implementing extended reality simulators into surgical training programs as an alternative or complement to dry lab training. The authors conclude that "extended reality simulators allow for an increase in variability in situation tasks and repeatability that these other models do not offer." XR training significantly improved time to complete versus no training and produced comparable results to dry lab training on both outcome measures.
requirements: Simulators must produce objective measures of performance and allow real-time feedback to trainees.
constraints: The cost of a dVSS simulator is much less than a full da Vinci surgical robot, but still substantial (approximately $127,000).
key_sources: Bickford Michael, Alruwaili Fayez, Ragab Sara, Rothenberg Hanna, Abedin-Nasab Mohammad (2025). Impact of extended reality on robot-assisted surgery training: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-025-02559-z

article_title: Effectiveness of Constructivist Approach on Academic Achievement in Science at Secondary Level
citation: Samaresh Adak. (2017). Effectiveness of constructivist approach on academic achievement in science at secondary level. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2017.3298
title: Use the constructivist 7E model in secondary science teaching to develop higher achievement, especially for low- and average-intelligence students
description: The article recommends the constructivist 7E-model strategy for science teaching at secondary level because its trial produced significantly higher achievement than traditional teaching, with the largest gains among low- and average-intelligence students. The author states it is "recommended that constructivist 7E -model strategy be used in science teaching for the development of student’s higher achievement in science at secondary level" and that it gives scope for active participation and interaction with peers and teachers.
requirements: Teachers need to encourage peer interaction, group discussion, experimentation and field visiting; school administration should provide required learning resources
constraints: Evidence comes from one purposive sample of 58 students in two lessons of physical science at a single Bengali-medium school; the high-intelligence subgroup gain was not significant
target_learners: secondary school science students, including low- and average-intelligence students
target_learning_goals: higher achievement and mastery of science content at higher-order cognition levels
examples: The experimental section was taught two Class IX physical science lessons via 7E lesson plans and outperformed the traditionally taught control section on gain scores
key_sources: Samaresh Adak. (2017). Effectiveness of constructivist approach on academic achievement in science at secondary level. Educational Research and Reviews. https://doi.org/10.5897/ERR2017.3298

article_title: Academic Controversy in Macroeconomics: An Active and Collaborative Method to Increase Student Learning
citation: Craig F. Santicola. (2015). Academic Controversy In Macroeconomics: An Active And Collaborative Method To Increase Student Learning. American Journal Of Business Education – Third Quarter 2015 Volume 8, Number 3. https://www.clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE
title: Use academic controversy lessons instead of relying solely on passive lecture in post-secondary economics courses
description: The article recommends adopting academic controversy as an active, cooperative alternative to the passive lecture that dominates economics instruction, where surveys cited report roughly 83 percent of class time spent lecturing. Its own quasi-experimental evidence shows the controversy group significantly outperforming the lecture group on the TUCE, and the author concludes the technique "shows promise for improving the low learning outcomes identified in the literature."
requirements: Instructor training in the five-step controversy procedure and lesson pack preparation
Cooperative groups of four with pro/con pair structure and rubric-based scoring
constraints: Evidence base is a single small quasi-experiment (34 students) at one community college; the technique had not previously been examined in economics
examples: The study implemented eight academic controversy lessons across a spring 2010 semester, with an initial sample lesson to acclimate students to the format and the concept of civil discourse
key_sources: Craig F. Santicola. (2015). Academic Controversy In Macroeconomics: An Active And Collaborative Method To Increase Student Learning. American Journal Of Business Education – Third Quarter 2015 Volume 8, Number 3. https://www.clutejournals.com/index.php/AJBE

article_title: Examining the Effectiveness of Pre-Reading Strategies on Saudi EFL College Students' Reading Comprehension
citation: Hana S. S. Al Rasheed. (2014). Examining the Effectiveness of Pre-reading Strategies on Saudi EFL College Students' Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 7(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n11p79
title: Use pre-reading strategies in EFL reading lessons to activate prior knowledge and motivate students, while training students not to rely on knowing every word
description: The article recommends that EFL teachers employ pre-reading strategies—pre-questioning, vocabulary pre-teaching, having students write and answer their own questions, and suggesting vocabulary they might encounter—to familiarize students with text context and improve comprehension. It also recommends training students to guess or skip unknown words, since "Students do not need to understan d the meaning of every single word in the text." The study's null comparison shows the two tested strategies were equally effective, not that either is optimal.
requirements: Reading selections of a given level should be carefully chosen to be neither too difficult nor too easy, so passages provide comprehensible input
constraints: The study was limited to female undergraduates at King Saud University in 2011/2012, and its multiple-choice instruments allowed high chances of guessing, so findings cannot be over generalized; Stott (2001) warns against activating prior knowledge at the expense of foreign-language learning by overusing L1
examples: The researcher translated new vocabulary into Arabic with the vocabulary pre-teaching group for ten minutes and raised questions with the pre-questioning group before ten minutes of reading and answering eight comprehension questions
key_sources: Hana S. S. Al Rasheed. (2014). Examining the Effectiveness of Pre-reading Strategies on Saudi EFL College Students' Reading Comprehension. English Language Teaching, 7(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n11p79

article_title: Experimental Design: Utilizing Microsoft Mathematics in Teaching and Learning Calculus
citation: Rina Oktaviyanthi, Yani Supriani. (2015). Experimental Design: Utilizing Microsoft Mathematics in Teaching and Learning Calculus. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.25. https://www.iiste.org
title: Use interactive visualization software in Calculus teaching to improve achievement and attitudes
description: The article concludes that applying computer software, in this study Microsoft Mathematics, in the classroom is important to improve students' learning, because interactive visualization facilitates students to better understand mathematical content in ways not obtained with conventional teaching. It supports this with the experimental group's higher post-test achievement and with positive attitude questionnaire responses, and states the tool assists students to gain better understanding, enrich mathematics learning, and increase motivation to get more involved in learning activities.
requirements: Technology used for education purposes should be complemented with dynamic animation and flexible so that students can build understanding
constraints: Evidence comes from one small quasi-experiment with 22 students at a single university; the article notes most students' weakness was being only able to perform simple calculations
target_learners: first-year university students in Calculus courses
examples: The experimental group was taught using Microsoft Mathematics across drill-and-practice, parameter-variation, and conceptual-understanding activities, then compared with a conventionally taught control group on pre and post tests
key_sources: Rina Oktaviyanthi, Yani Supriani. (2015). Experimental Design: Utilizing Microsoft Mathematics in Teaching and Learning Calculus. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.25. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1078520

article_title: Effects of Concept Mapping Instruction Approach on Students' Achievement in Basic Science
citation: Ukpai Patricia Ogonnaya, Gabriel Okafor, Okechukwu S. Abonyi, J.O Ugama. (2016). Effects of Concept Mapping Instruction Approach on Students’ Achievement in Basic Science. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.8. https://www.iiste.org
title: Use concept mapping for teaching basic science to both male and female students
description: Based on the finding that concept mapping raised achievement with no gender differential and no interaction, the authors recommend that "Concept mapping therefore, should be used for teaching both male and female students in basic science." They argue the method presents topics bit by bit from known to unknown, shows meaningful relationships between concepts, promotes creative thinking in both male and female students, and takes care of individual differences.
requirements: Instruction should link concepts and move from known to unknown, as the article describes concept mapping doing
constraints: Evidence base is a single quasi-experiment in two coeducational schools in Ebonyi State, Nigeria
examples: The quasi-experiment assigned one school to concept mapping and one to conventional teaching via a coin toss and compared adjusted posttest means.
key_sources: Ukpai Patricia Ogonnaya, Gabriel Okafor, Okechukwu S. Abonyi, J.O Ugama. (2016). Effects of Concept Mapping Instruction Approach on Students’ Achievement in Basic Science. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.8. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1095361

article_title: Third Graders' Understanding of Air Concepts Facilitated by the iPod Inquiry Teaching Method
citation: Lai, C. (2016). Third graders' understanding of air concepts facilitated by the iPod inquiry teaching method. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 2(1), 1-9. https://www.ijres.net
title: Use iPod inquiry teaching for primary school science units
description: On the basis of the study's results, the article concludes that the iPod inquiry teaching method is suitable for primary school science teaching: it enhances learning motives, strengthens thinking skills, deepens peer discussions, and promotes construction of scientific concepts, while its diversified activities stimulate enthusiasm for exploration and offer instant communication and mutual feedback. The recommendation rests on the two ANCOVA findings in this single quasi-experiment.
requirements: Teachers implement all four steps (invitation, prediction, operation, discussion) with the stated principles
Teaching hours and content are held equal across compared groups
constraints: Evidence base is one quasi-experimental study of one air concept unit with third graders in New Taipei City
examples: The study compared iPod inquiry teaching with regular textbook teaching for the Kang-Hsuan 'Invisible Air' unit, three 40-minute classes a week for a total of 12 classes
key_sources: Lai, C. (2016). Third graders' understanding of air concepts facilitated by the iPod inquiry teaching method. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 2(1), 1-9. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105183

article_title: The Effect of Flipped Classroom Model on Students' Classroom Engagement in Teaching English
citation: Ayçiçek, B., & Yanpar Yelken, T. (2018). The Effect of Flipped Classroom Model on Students’ Classroom Engagement in Teaching English. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 385-398. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11226a
title: Use the flipped classroom model to enhance classroom engagement, with teacher preparation and technical capacity planning
description: Based on the finding that the flipped classroom group's engagement rose while the control group's did not, the article concludes that "teachers can be suggested to use flipped classroom model to enhance classroom engagement". Its implementation suggestions are that "Teachers should be informed about the model and motivated to use technology", that seminars and workshops be organized to spread the model, and that the technical capacity of the learning environment be planned well to make class processes more efficient. It also recommends providing course contents on CD, DVD or portable memory to students with internet access problems.
requirements: Teachers informed about the model and motivated to use technology; well-planned technical capacity of the learning environment
constraints: The study was a four-week application in one secondary school English course with 40 seventh-grade students; the authors call for studying the model at other education levels and courses
examples: The experimental group's English course was flipped for four weeks using instructor-made videos and Edpuzzle, and its engagement gains exceeded the control group's
key_sources: Ayçiçek, B., & Yanpar Yelken, T. (2018). The Effect of Flipped Classroom Model on Students’ Classroom Engagement in Teaching English. International Journal of Instruction, 11(2), 385-398. https://doi.org/10.12973/iji.2018.11226a

article_title: The Effects of Two Teachers' Instructional Methods on Students' Learning Outcomes in Chemistry in Selected Senior Secondary School in Kaduna Metropolis, Nigeria
citation: Efe M. Omwirhiren, Khalil U. Ibrahim. (2016). The Effects of Two Teachers' Instructional Methods on Students' Learning Outcomes in Chemistry in Selected Senior Secondary School in Kaduna Metropolis, Nigeria. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.15. https://www.iiste.org
title: Incorporate the demonstration method in senior secondary chemistry teaching to enhance academic performance
description: The article recommends that chemistry teachers replace predominantly lecture-based instruction with the demonstration method, a practical approach that "involves showing, doing and telling something", in which the teacher displays and explains the steps of a process while students practice by repeating what the teacher has done. The study's post-test results are offered as the empirical basis for this recommendation.
requirements: Teachers need the ability to display the steps in a process and explain them accurately and clearly while students practice
constraints: The authors state the results apply to public secondary schools in Kaduna metropolis and cannot say whether the relationships apply to other institutions of secondary education
target_learners: Senior secondary (SS II) science students, ages 16-20
target_learning_goals: Understanding of chemical bonding topics: forces within molecules, ionic bond, covalent bond, overlaps of atomic orbitals, bond polarity, metallic bond, intermolecular forces
examples: In the study, the experimental group of fifty students was exposed to demonstration method and the control group of fifty to lecture method for three weeks on chemical bonding, with post-tests compared via t-test and ANOVA.
key_sources: Efe M. Omwirhiren, Khalil U. Ibrahim. (2016). The Effects of Two Teachers' Instructional Methods on Students' Learning Outcomes in Chemistry in Selected Senior Secondary School in Kaduna Metropolis, Nigeria. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.15. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1103149

article_title: Effects of Two and Three-Dimensional Visual Objects on the Acquisition of Drawing Skills among JSS1 Students in Osun State, Nigeria
citation: Bada Tayo Abass, Bello Isyakka, Ijisakin Yemi Olaolu & Fajuyigbe Michael Olusegun. (2014). Effects of Two and Three-Dimensional Visual Objects on the Acquisition of Drawing Skills among JSS1 Students in Osun State, Nigeria. World Journal of Education, 4(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v4n1p62
title: Use two- and three-dimensional visual objects in junior secondary drawing instruction
description: The article recommends that basic drawing be taught with concrete two- and three-dimensional visual objects rather than by conventional expository teaching alone, because in its experiment both visual-object groups outperformed the control group. It concludes that "the use of two and three dimensional objects will anhance drawing skills" and that visual objects make "the instructional content is more real and delivered with vigour". Three-dimensional objects produced the highest scores, so they are the preferred option where available.
requirements: Teachers need access to two- and three-dimensional visual objects; the article notes Fine Arts "lacks materials such as 2 dimensional and 3 dimensional visual objects, charts, display boards, films, and filmstrips, slides, video" in many schools.
constraints: Evidence comes from one purposively selected sample of three schools and 120 JSS1 students in Atakumosa Local Government Area, Osun State, Nigeria; the article does not claim generalization beyond this setting.
examples: In the study, experimental group A was taught with three-dimensional visual objects, group B with two-dimensional visual objects, and the control group by conventional classroom method, all covering the same contents and number of lessons.
key_sources: Bada Tayo Abass, Bello Isyakka, Ijisakin Yemi Olaolu & Fajuyigbe Michael Olusegun. (2014). Effects of Two and Three-Dimensional Visual Objects on the Acquisition of Drawing Skills among JSS1 Students in Osun State, Nigeria. World Journal of Education, 4(1). https://doi.org/10.5430/wje.v4n1p62

article_title: Demonstration Technique to Improve Vocabulary and Grammar Element in Teaching Speaking at EFL Learners
citation: Muhammad Husnu. (2018). Demonstration Technique to Improve Vocabulary and Grammar Element in Teaching Speaking at EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 11(2). http://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p26
title: Teachers should use the demonstration technique to teach speaking to EFL learners
description: The article concludes that demonstration technique is significantly effective for improving the vocabulary and grammar elements of speaking at EFL learners and states that "the teacher should use the demonstration technique to teach speaking." It works by giving simple materials and practice, with learning dominated by demonstration and interaction among learners, so words are used in real practice rather than only learned as meanings. The article reports it made learning more interesting and raised student motivation and enthusiasm.
requirements: Demonstration and interaction among learners dominate the learning process, with words used in real practice
constraints: Evidence comes from a single true-experimental study of second-semester Economic Department students at one Indonesian university
target_learners: EFL learners at the beginner level
examples: The study gave pre-test, demonstration-technique treatment, and post-test to 32 experimental students, whose mean rose from 2.01 to 4.01 while the control group's rose only from 2.07 to 2.7.
key_sources: Muhammad Husnu. (2018). Demonstration Technique to Improve Vocabulary and Grammar Element in Teaching Speaking at EFL Learners. English Language Teaching, 11(2). http://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n2p26

article_title: Effects of Computer-Assisted STAD, LTM and ICI Cooperative Learning Strategies on Nigerian Secondary School Students' Achievement, Gender and Motivation in Physics
citation: Amosa Isiaka Gambari, Mudasiru Olalere Yusuf, David Akpa Thomas. (2015). Effects of Computer-Assisted STAD, LTM and ICI Cooperative Learning Strategies on Nigerian Secondary School Students' Achievement, Gender and Motivation in Physics. The Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Science, Volume 3, Issue 4. https://www.moj-es.net
title: Use computer-assisted STAD cooperative teaching to enhance achievement, retention and motivation in physics
description: The article recommends that physics teachers adopt the computer-assisted STAD cooperative strategy, in which students work in heterogeneous three-member groups with assigned roles, team quizzes and team scores, supported by an instructional package with animated illustration and audio narration. It states "Physics teachers should be encouraged to use computer-assisted STAD cooperative teaching strategy to enhance students' academic achievement, retention and motivation in physics." The recommendation rests on the study's finding that STAD outperformed individualized computer instruction.
requirements: Teachers and students require training; participants "were trained for two weeks" with an operational guide provided.
The computer-assisted instructional package must present content with animation and immediate feedback before students proceed to the next unit.
constraints: Evidence comes from one four-week study in three purposively sampled secondary schools in Minna, Nigeria, on SSII Structure of Matter content.
target_learning_goals: Physics achievement in Structure of Matter concepts
examples: Students in three-member heterogeneous groups with roles (group leader, time-keeper, scribe/quiet captain) completed CAIP materials together, took team quizzes by consensus, and received team scores counting equally with individual quiz scores toward the final grade.
key_sources: Amosa Isiaka Gambari, Mudasiru Olalere Yusuf, David Akpa Thomas. (2015). Effects of Computer-Assisted STAD, LTM and ICI Cooperative Learning Strategies on Nigerian Secondary School Students' Achievement, Gender and Motivation in Physics. The Malaysian Online Journal of Educational Science, Volume 3, Issue 4. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085925

article_title: The Use of Manipulatives in Mathematics Education
citation: Ernest Larbi, Okyere Mavis. (2016). The Use of Manipulatives in Mathematics Education. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.36. https://www.iiste.org
title: Use algebra tiles when introducing students to algebraic concepts, emphasising process over product
description: The article recommends algebra tiles as a tool for introducing algebraic concepts, particularly for teaching the distributive property so students discover the pattern in removing brackets from an expression. It advises that "emphasis must be laid on 'process' and not 'product'", and that mathematics educators should use manipulatives such as algebra tiles for effective teaching of all algebra units. Lessons with manipulatives are said to serve auditory, visual and kinesthetic learners alike.
requirements: Teachers must lay emphasis on process rather than product when using tiles to teach the distributive property
constraints: The study was conducted using only two schools, which the authors state makes it difficult to generalise the results
target_learners: Junior high school students beginning algebra
target_learning_goals: Conceptual understanding of basic algebra operations
examples: The study's experimental group used algebra tiles across four weeks of algebra instruction and outperformed the conventionally taught control group on the posttest
key_sources: Ernest Larbi, Okyere Mavis. (2016). The Use of Manipulatives in Mathematics Education. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.36. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1126428

article_title: The Effect of Peer Teaching on Mathematics Academic Achievement of the Undergraduate Students in Oman
citation: Abdelkarim, R., & Abuiyada, R. (2016). The Effect of Peer Teaching on Mathematics Academic Achievement of the Undergraduate Students in Oman. International Education Studies, 9(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n5p124
title: Instructors should use peer teaching to help students increase their mathematics achievement
description: Based on the finding that the peer-teaching group significantly outperformed the control group, the article recommends that "the in structors and college professors to use peer teaching as a very good strategy to help students in increasing their achievement". Peer teaching is presented as an inexpensive strategy that engages students actively rather than leaving them as passive recipients under traditional lecturing.
requirements: A qualified peer teacher who has previously mastered the course content
Teacher supervision available to resolve problems between students
constraints: Evidence base is a single small study of 32 female undergraduates in one mathematics course at one university
examples: The study assigned low-scoring students to discussion groups supported by a former student who scored above 95% in the course
key_sources: Abdelkarim, R., & Abuiyada, R. (2016). The Effect of Peer Teaching on Mathematics Academic Achievement of the Undergraduate Students in Oman. International Education Studies, 9(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n5p124

article_title: Using Video Materials in English for Technical Sciences: A Case Study
citation: Milosevic, D. (2017). Using video materials in English for technical sciences: a case study. In C. Sarré & S. Whyte (Eds), New developments in ESP teaching and learning research (pp. 15-30). Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2017.cssw2017.743
title: Use audio-visual materials in ESP classes to clarify complex subject-matter and increase student motivation
description: The article advocates for a more extensive use of audio-visual material in ESP practice, arguing that AVRs "create a concrete basis for conceptual thinking" and "make abstract ideas more concrete to learners". Videos present concrete examples through linguistic and non-linguistic cues, eliminating abstraction from language and making technical content easier to grasp and memorise.
requirements: Materials must be properly selected to bring real life into the classroom and present students with every-day professional situations
constraints: Implementation may be limited by shortage of time, inadequacy of equipment, or insufficient computer literacy of teachers
target_learners: first-year university students in technical sciences
examples: The study used a Samsung cartoon advertisement about AMOLED displays as video material and two internet texts as reading material, teaching a 45-minute ESP unit on mobile technology.
key_sources: Milosevic, D. (2017). Using video materials in English for technical sciences: a case study. In C. Sarré & S. Whyte (Eds), New developments in ESP teaching and learning research (pp. 15-30). Research-publishing.net. https://doi.org/10.14705/rpnet.2017.cssw2017.743

article_title: Efficacy of Enrichment Triad and Self-Direct Models on Academic Achievement of Gifted Students in Selected Secondary Schools in Nigeria
citation: Fakolade, O. A. & Adeniyi, S. A. (2010). Efficacy of Enrichment Triad and Self-Direct Models on Academic Achievement of Gifted Students in Selected Secondary Schools in Nigeria. International Journal of Special Education, Vol 25 No 1. https://www.internationaljournalofspecialeducation.com
title: Regular and special educators should use Enrichment Triad and Self-Directed models to facilitate gifted students' academic achievement
description: The article concludes that because "the Enrichment Triad and Self-Directed models are capable of facilitating gifted students' educational programmes," both regular and special educators should adopt them for gifted learners. It argues conventional or traditional methods currently used in Nigerian schools cannot provide the challenge gifted children need, and advocates combining models into a comprehensive approach, including Renzulli's suggestion to combine enrichment activities with other process models.
requirements: Educators must come to understand their potential role in enhancing creativity, divergent thinking, and intellectual and academic achievement in gifted children
constraints: The recommendation is grounded in one quasi-experimental study of 75 gifted students in Oyo State, Nigeria
examples: The study exposed gifted students to 13 weeks of Enrichment Triad and Self-Directed sessions in English and Mathematics and found significant treatment effects favoring both models over conventional instruction
key_sources: Fakolade, O. A. & Adeniyi, S. A. (2010). Efficacy of Enrichment Triad and Self-Direct Models on Academic Achievement of Gifted Students in Selected Secondary Schools in Nigeria. International Journal of Special Education, Vol 25 No 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ890561

article_title: Effects of Graphic Organiser on Students' Achievement in Algebraic Word Problems
citation: Josiah Owolabi & Tobiloba Faith Adaramati. (2015). Effects of Graphic Organiser on Students' Achievement in Algebraic Word Problems. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.5. http://www.iiste.org
title: Use graphic organisers, and prefer having students design their own, when teaching algebraic word problems
description: The article recommends graphic organisers as a more effective approach than the conventional lecture method for teaching mathematics concepts in Nigerian secondary schools. It concludes that "the group that were taught to design graphic organise r (Experimental group B) did better than the first ex perimental group that used already prepared graphic organiser", and encourages teachers to source templates and software such as Kidspiration and Inspiration.
requirements: Teachers need access to graphic organiser templates or software such as Kidspiration and Inspiration to support classroom use.
constraints: The evidence comes from a small non-equivalent group study in one Lagos college; the approach is described as not largely used in Nigerian secondary schools.
examples: Experimental group A was taught using the graphic organiser and given blank organisers for exercises, while Experimental group B was taught how to design one; the control group received conventional teaching.
key_sources: Josiah Owolabi & Tobiloba Faith Adaramati. (2015). Effects of Graphic Organiser on Students' Achievement in Algebraic Word Problems. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.5. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1083649

article_title: Effects of Applying Blogs to Assist Life Education Instruction for Elementary School Students
citation: Lou, S.-J., Kao, M.-C., Yen, H.-L., & Shih, R.-C. (2013). Effects of applying blogs to assist life education instruction for elementary school students. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(4). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Uschool blog platform with e-portfolio scoring for blog-assisted life education
description: Uschool served as "a blog platform for the students to share outlines and reflections on the 10 themes of life education." Students posted learning records containing teaching materials, their own articles, instructor feedback and fine works. Blog articles were scored on a 5-point Likert scale across three domains—organization, content and creativity—by the instructor and a senior instructor; Spearman Rank Correlation scores "reached the significance level of .05, indicating the two scorers’ scorings were consistent."
requirements: Students must be able to publish outlines and articles and read other groups' articles on the platform
Two scorers establish inter-rater consistency for portfolio scoring
constraints: The e-portfolio scoring was applied to the 10 articles on the blogs of 7 different groups in this single class
target_learners: fifth-grade elementary school students in heterogeneous groups
examples: An entry page and a sample of a teacher's comment and a student's follow-up feedback are shown in Figures 3 and 4
key_sources: Lou, S.-J., Kao, M.-C., Yen, H.-L., & Shih, R.-C. (2013). Effects of applying blogs to assist life education instruction for elementary school students. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 12(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1018031

article_title: The Effect of Listening to Music on Iranian Children's Segmental and Suprasegmental Pronunciation
citation: Fereshteh Moradi & Mohsen Shahrokhi. (2014). The Effect of Listening to Music on Iranian Children's Segmental and Suprasegmental Pronunciation. English Language Teaching, 7(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n6p128
title: Use music to draw learners' attention to correct pronunciation, stress and intonation in EFL teaching for children
description: The article recommends music as a helpful instructional medium for pronunciation teaching: "The main implication of this study is that music can be used as a helpful way to draw learners' attention to the correct form of the sounds and pronunciation." It argues music motivates imitation of the singer's sounds, provides a relaxed atmosphere where learners speak without fear of criticism, and helps teachers address learners' lack of interest in pronunciation work. The recommendation rests on the study's significant posttest differences favoring the music group.
requirements: Songs whose words and sentences contain the target pronunciation features, so test and practice items are drawn from the songs themselves
constraints: Evidence comes from one small quasi-experiment with 30 female beginner children in Isfahan; the article notes only female students took part due to limited access to both genders
examples: The article also recommends that "Practitioners who work on developing language materials are also welcome to include explicit exercises on songs and language learning" so learners improve both production and comprehension of sounds.
key_sources: Fereshteh Moradi & Mohsen Shahrokhi. (2014). The Effect of Listening to Music on Iranian Children's Segmental and Suprasegmental Pronunciation. English Language Teaching, 7(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n6p128

article_title: Exploring the Use of Online Educational Platform in Teaching Writing among ESL Students
citation: Topacio, K. N. M. (2018). Exploring the use of online educational platform in teaching writing among ESL students. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 14(1), 86-101. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1189264
title: UST E-Leap learning management software for online writing instruction
description: UST E-Leap is a web-based course/learning management software (LMS) administered by the University of Santo Tomas that includes "announcement and discussion boards, class notes, traditional assessment tools like quizzes and examination, and score sheets or books." In this study it delivered ten writing lessons through PowerPoint and video presentations, with assignments submitted and evaluated online.
requirements: Internet access for all students
Instructor presence to post lessons, moderate discussions, and evaluate submissions
constraints: Dormitory-based students with limited internet access were disenfranchised; final paper still submitted as hard copy for inter-rating
target_learning_goals: Argumentative essay writing through process writing approach
examples: Lessons were given through PowerPoint presentations with video uploads in the class notes area; students checked announcement boards for new assignments
key_sources: Topacio, K. N. M. (2018). Exploring the use of online educational platform in teaching writing among ESL students. Journal of Language and Linguistic Studies, 14(1), 86-101. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1175799

article_title: Visual Representations in Mathematics Teaching: An Experiment with Students
citation: Debrenti, E. (2015). Visual Representations in Mathematics Teaching: An Experiment with Students. Acta Didactica Napocensia, 8(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ
title: Use concrete and visual representations in mathematics teaching to facilitate problem understanding and solution.
description: The article argues there is "a strong need for the use of concrete and visual representations in the teaching of mathematics in schools." Visual representations such as sketches, drawings, cards, and computer models help students understand problem structure, relate known and unknown quantities, and devise solution strategies for word problems.
requirements: Teachers must introduce representations through practice and make students aware of their use, with patience.
constraints: Computer-delivered representations may not sustain motivation as well as physical manipulables; the computer group showed decreased interest and fatigue.
examples: 57 economics freshmen solved an Einstein-type logic puzzle using paper, physical cards, or a computer program with virtual cards.
key_sources: Debrenti, E. (2015). Visual Representations in Mathematics Teaching: An Experiment with Students. Acta Didactica Napocensia, 8(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1064387

article_title: Teaching to Diversity: Creating Compassionate Learning Communities for Diverse Elementary School Students
citation: Katz, J., & Porath, M. (2011). Teaching to diversity: Creating compassionate learning communities for diverse elementary school students. International Journal of Special Education, 26(2), 29–39. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ966542
title: Use a multiple intelligences framework to facilitate social and emotional learning and build self and social respect.
description: The article argues that an MI framework is useful for SEL because it provides teachers with neutral, non-culturally biased language, fits within teachers' skill sets, and allows integration of SEL into academic curricula. The RD program used this framework to help students explore diversity, differentiate instruction, and build self and social respect. The framework was chosen despite controversy in the field, for its intuitive utility in differentiating instruction and its cross-cultural basis.
requirements: Teachers need training in MI theory and support to extend the framework across the curriculum
constraints: MI theory is controversial in the field; the article uses it as a tool rather than endorsing its scientific status
target_learners: elementary school students in Grades four to seven

The validated P‐UGVA Rating Scale for the 1–1 objective assessment

description: A 15-criterion evaluation framework, adapted by Renaud from ergonomic psychology and design ergonomics, organized into three dimensions: usability (five indicators A1–A5, e.g. ease of understanding, workload, flexibility), usefulness (six indicators B1–B6, e.g. relevance of objectives, student engagement, observed progress) and acceptability (four indicators C1–C4, e.g. compatibility with ethics and teaching style).
